unit.title: Word Formation & Derivation
unit.subtitle: Prefixes, suffixes and the cultismo/patrimonial split

grammar.title: Build and decode any word like a native
grammar.intro: At C2 you stop looking words up and start deriving them. Spanish is astonishingly regular: strip a prefix like des- or re-, recognise a suffix like -ción or -miento, and an unfamiliar word becomes transparent. Master the machinery and you can both decode a word you have never seen and coin one that sounds native.

sections.heading: Prefixes: negation, repetition, excess
sections.body: The most productive prefixes cluster by meaning. Negation: des- (deshacer), in-/im-/i- (inútil, imposible, ilegal) — note the assimilation to im- before p/b and i- before l/r. Repetition or intensity: re- (rehacer, requetebueno). Excess: sobre-/super- (sobrevalorar, superpoblado). Position and opposition: pre-, pos(t)-, anti-, contra-, sub-, entre-.
conj: útil → inútil, posible → imposible, legal → ilegal

ex.en: It's unwise to overvalue the first draft.

ex.es: Tuvo que rehacer el informe de cero.
ex.en: He had to redo the report from scratch.

sections.heading: Suffixes: turning verbs and adjectives into nouns
sections.body: Suffixes carry the grammatical weight. Actions become nouns with -ción/-sión (crear → creación) or -miento (crecer → crecimiento). Qualities become abstract nouns with -dad/-tad (feliz → felicidad, leal → lealtad), -ez/-eza (rígido → rigidez, bello → belleza) and -ura (dulce → dulzura). And people become agents with -dor/-dora (jugar → jugador).

sections.heading: Chaining affixes to coin words
sections.body: Real fluency is combining pieces. From feliz you get felicidad, and adding negation gives infelicidad. From hacer you reach deshacer, rehacer and the noun deshacerse de. The suffix -mente then turns adjectives into adverbs, always attaching to the feminine form: rápida → rápidamente.

ex.en: The unpredictability of the market scares him.
He acted irresponsibly and he knows it.

sections.heading: Cultismo vs patrimonial: the learned doublets
sections.body: Many Latin roots entered Spanish twice: once through centuries of popular speech (the voz patrimonial, worn down by sound change) and once borrowed straight from Latin by scholars (the cultismo, closer to the original). This is why colocar and colgar both come from collocare, and cátedra and cadera both from cathedra. The cultismo usually sounds more formal or technical.

ex.es: Prefiere colocar los libros; yo solo los cuelgo del clavo.
ex.en: He prefers to arrange the books; I just hang them on the nail.

ex.es: Ganó la cátedra tras años de esfuerzo.
ex.en: She won the professorship after years of effort.

takeaways: des-/in-(im-/i-) negate; re- repeats or intensifies; sobre-/super- mark excess.
in- assimilates: im- before p/b (imposible), i- before l/r (ilegal, irreal).
Cultismo/patrimonial doublets (colocar/colgar, cátedra/cadera) share one Latin root; the cultismo is more formal.

mistakes.why: in- assimilates to im- before p and b: imposible, not inposible.
-mente attaches to the feminine adjective: rápida → rápidamente.

mistakes.w: Admiro su liderato en el equipo.
mistakes.r: Admiro su liderazgo en el equipo.
mistakes.why: The productive noun from líder is liderazgo (with -azgo), not the calqued 'liderato' in this sense.

exercises.prompt: Antes de firmar, no conviene ___ el riesgo real del proyecto.
exercises.prompt_en: Before signing, it's unwise to underestimate the project's real risk.
exercises.no: To under-value is “infravalorar” (infra- = below), not invalorar.

exercises.prompt: Su respuesta fue totalmente ___; nadie la esperaba.
exercises.prompt_en: His answer was completely unpredictable; nobody expected it.
exercises.no: Before p the prefix becomes im-: “imprevisible”, not inprevisible.

exercises.prompt: Build: "The company's sustained growth surprised everyone."
exercises.no: The noun is “crecimiento” (crecer + -miento) — mind the i before -miento.

exercises.prompt: El error era grave, así que tuvo que ___ todo el documento. (hacer, otra vez)
exercises.prompt_en: The mistake was serious, so he had to redo the whole document.

exercises.prompt: Match each base word to its correct derived noun.

exercises.tts: Colocar y colgar vienen de la misma raíz latina.
accepted: colocar y colgar vienen de la misma raiz latina
exercises.translation: Colocar and colgar come from the same Latin root.
exercises.no: It was: “Colocar y colgar vienen de la misma raíz latina.” (a learned/inherited doublet).

exercises.scenario: Two editors discuss why one word sounds more formal 📚

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.es: ¿Por qué “cátedra” suena tan culto y “cadera” tan cotidiano, si vienen de lo mismo?
lines.en: Why does “cátedra” sound so learned and “cadera” so everyday, if they come from the same word?

options.text: Porque “cadera” es la voz patrimonial, gastada por el uso, y “cátedra” es el cultismo tomado directamente del latín.
Porque “cátedra” es más nueva y alguien la inventó en el siglo pasado.
Porque en realidad no tienen nada que ver: son raíces distintas por casualidad parecidas.

exercises.ok: ¡Perfecto! Esa es exactamente la distinción culto/patrimonial.
exercises.no: The formal one is the cultismo taken straight from Latin; the everyday one is the worn-down voz patrimonial — option a.

exercises.say: Tuvo que rehacer el informe porque lo había sobrevalorado.
exercises.en: He had to redo the report because he had overvalued it.
exercises.no: Almost — tap “Hear it”, then match the rhythm of “Tuvo que rehacer el informe porque lo había sobrevalorado.”

inherited word worn down by popular speech
